A PUF-Based Approach for Copy Protection of
Intellectual Property in Neural Network Models⋆
Daniel Dorfmeister, Flavio Ferrarotti, Bernhard Fischer,
Martin Schwandtner, Hannes Sochor
Software Competence Center Hagenberg, Softwarepark 32a, 4232 Hagenberg, Austria
<firstname>.<lastname>@scch.at
Abstract. More and more companies’ Intellectual Property (IP) is being
integrated into Neural Network (NN) models. This IP has considerable
value for companies and, therefore, requires adequate protection. For
example, an attacker might replicate a production machines’ hardware
and subsequently simply copy associated software and NN models onto
the cloned hardware. To make copying NN models onto cloned hard-
ware infeasible, we present an approach to bind NN models—and thus
also the IP contained within them—to their underlying hardware. For
this purpose, we link an NN model’s weights, which are crucial for its
operation, to unique and unclonable hardware properties by leveraging
Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs). By doing so, sufficient accuracy
can only be achieved using the target hardware to restore the original
weights, rendering proper execution of the NN model on cloned hardware
impossible. We demonstrate that our approach accomplishes the desired
degradation of accuracy on various NN models and outline possible future
improvements.
Key words:neural networks, intellectual property protection, physically
unclonable functions, hardware-software binding
1 Introduction
Neural Network (NN) models are increasingly deployed in all areas, including
industry. For instance, they are readily applied for quality optimisation and
process automation in diverse industrial machines. To make this possible, a
considerable amount of resources, including time and money, are being invested
in the development of NN models, which therefore increasingly incorporate the
core Intellectual Property (IP) of companies. In this context, it is important
to ensure the privacy of the training data of the models, i.e., to prevent the

extraction of the original data from the models. An important effort is indeed
being made to deal with this problem (see, e.g., [11]).
However, a rather neglected aspect is the fact that NN models can be easily
copied and used without due authorisation. This is known as software piracy and
comprises the unauthorised copy, use, download, and distribution of software. In
this sense, a pre-trained NN model is not different to classical software, beyond
the fact that it is learned instead of programmed. We can differentiate among
end-user, online and commercial piracy. End-user piracy occurs when the software
lacks copy protection and end-users illegally redistribute it in their private circle.
Online piracy is the distribution of pirated software online via a central server or
a peer-to-peer file sharing platform. Commercial piracy refers to an organisation
that pirates software to gain a financial advantage, mainly by counterfeiting
and then reselling it as original software or as part of a product that uses this
software. The main motivations for software piracy and their consequences for
companies are well documented for a long time [ 14]. For all types of software
piracy, the main problem is inadequate copy protection [4].
In an industrial setting, the lack of copy protection built into NNs means
that it is often not even necessary to know anything about a NN model, but it is
enough to simply make a copy of it in order to profit at the expense of the IP
owner. In Germany alone, it is estimated that product or brand piracy accounts
for an annual loss of 6.4 billion euros2. The main effort when stealing IP from
production machines is primarily in reverse engineering and cloning the hardware,
as software and NN models can be simply copied.
In this paper, we propose a possible solution to the described problem. Our
solution differs from classical copy protection mechanisms, usually based on
passwords or hardware dongles, as it is well known that they are rather easy to
circumvent, and can also be expensive if done properly. We follow an approach
based on binding a given NN model to a specific target machine so that its
accuracy is reduced when copied (without authorisation) and used on a different
machine. We choose a protection approach based on making the copied NN model
inaccurate instead of straight out unusable, as it can make the protection less
obvious and thus more difficult to break for an attacker. At the same time, this
reduces the runtime overhead of authorised uses of the protected model.

In order to achieve the binding between a NN model and a target machine, i.e.,
the machine where the model is authorised to run on, we must be able to uniquely
identify the underlying hardware. In the project DEPS3(short forDependable
Production Environments with Software Security) we are exploring different
ways of achieving precisely this objective. In particular, a promising approach to
software-hardware binding is the use of Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs),
a hardware-based security primitive. This primitive arises from the fact that each
circuit has unique physical properties resulting from unintended variations in
the manufacturing process. Consequently, these physical properties function as a
digital fingerprint that cannot be easily cloned, which is the basis for PUFs. PUFs
can either use dedicated hardware or components already present in systems,
such as DRAM.
Figure 1 illustrates this general idea: We have an industrial machine, e.g., a
robot arm with a neural network-based adaptive control method for trajectory
tracking [ 19]. To protect it from being copied and used without authorisation, a
fingerprint is taken from the industrial machine and tied to the neural network.
More precisely, several weights of the NN model are bound to the fingerprint in
such a way that the NN model can only provide sufficient accuracy on the basis
of this fingerprint. If such an industrial machine is now cloned and the protected
NN model linked to the original hardware is copied to this cloned machine, the
underlying fingerprint is now different and the NN model therefore no longer
provides sufficient accuracy.
Figure 2 exemplifies the impact of our protection method on the accuracy
of unauthorised copies of a NN model. The protected target machine classifies
the pictures of a dog and a cat correctly, while the two pirated copies cannot

verify the fingerprint (via the PUF) and thus classify them incorrectly. Note that
incorrect classifications might vary from one unauthorised copy to another. This
is because the fingerprint (PUF response) will differ between machines due to
the unique physical characteristics of the individual cloned machines (see, e.g.,
cloned machines 1 and 2). That is, if an adversary clones a machine and copies
the protected NN model, then it will no longer work as reliable as on the target
machine.
The paper is organised as follows: In the next section, we briefly introduce
the necessary background on NNs and PUFs, and fix the notation. In Section 3,
we specify the threat model assumptions. Our main contribution is condensed in
Sections 4–7 where we, respectively, introduce our novel protection mechanism, a
corresponding proof of concept strategy and implementation, associated experi-
mental results, and discuss our findings and current limitations of the approach.
The final two Sections, 8 and 9, are reserved for related work and the conclusion,
respectively.
2 Preliminaries
In this section, we provide the necessary background regarding neural network
models and physically unclonable functions, and we fix the notation used through-
out the paper.
2.1 Neural Networks
There are many different kinds of (artificial) Neural Networks (NNs) such as feed
forward (a.k.a. multilayer perceptrons), recurrent, and convolutional NNs. All
have in common that their architecture can be defined by some type of directed
graph with a set of nodes V, set of edges E⊆V×V and functions ( av)v∈V,
where for every node v∈V (usually excluding the input nodes), av:R→R is a
continuous function known asactivation functionat v. A concrete NN model
associates this skeleton architecture with aweight we∈Rwith every edge e∈E
and abias bvwith every node v∈V . NN models compute functions, but the way
in which this is done varies depending on the type of NN used. A constant in this
sense is that the computation takes place in the nodes and is propagated through
the graph, using the activation functions, weights and biases. The weight and
biases are learned from data. We are not concerned with the learning process itself
but with protecting the IP produced by this process in the form of a pre-trained
model. Thus, it make sense to encrypt the weights in the pre-trained model so
that an adversary cannot simply copy and use it without permission.
2.2 Physically Unclonable Functions
A Physically Unclonable Function (PUF) fis a function defined using unique
physically properties of hardware that cannot be cloned. Typically, it takes a

A PUF-Based Approach for Copy Protection of IP in NN Models 5
binary string bas input (challenge) and returns a possibly different binary string
b′as output (response). For each binary string bin the domain of f, there is a
corresponding b′=f(b), which is unique for the hardware of the target machine
M. More concretely, if fis a PUF, f(b) will be interpreted at run-time as b′only
if challenged on M. Otherwise, the response value f(b) will be arbitrary, and it
can be assumed thatf(b)̸=b′for almost all machinesM′different fromM.
There is a variety of PUFs that can be used in the context of the protection
proposed in this paper. For instance, in our project DEPS, we are experimenting
with DRAM PUFs [ 5], where the PUF response f(b) =b′to a challenge bis
the result of applying the Rowhammer exploit to flip some bits of b, which is
predictable in certain locations of the target DRAM. Many other alternatives exist,
e.g., arbiter PUFs, SRAM PUFs, ring oscillator PUFs, and optical PUFs [ 10,1].
Any of these alternatives can be used for implementing the copy protection
approach that we propose in this paper. The choice depends on the available
PUFs for the hardware where the trained NN model will be used, as well as the
response time and level of strength provided by the available options. This is
application-specific and should be evaluated on a case by case basis.
3 Threat Model
In this paper, we only consider attacks that aim to remove the copy protection of
the NN model, e.g., through reverse engineering. We assume that an attacker can
gain access to a model, e.g., via an update mechanism, backup of the machine,
or download of the firmware from the machine. We do not consider attacks on
hardware such as side-channel attacks or other attack vectors, e.g., supply chain
attacks. This also means that we are currently looking at a mere static attacker.
This attacker has access to only the model and all the information it contains
and can, therefore, not query the PUF and thus obtain Challenge-Response Pairs
(CRPs). However, we assume that our encryption method is public knowledge,
as security through obscurity would be bad practice. Both static and dynamic
analysis are described below. The focus of protection against dynamic analysis is
future work and will be discussed in Section 7.
3.1 Static Analysis
Using static analysis, an attacker does not execute the software—including NN
models—to be analysed but has access to the binary, potentially also to the
source code of the software. Thus, an attacker has access to all the information
that is present while the program is not running.
For example, a piece of software uses an NN model and requires a key for
decryption of the model’s encrypted weights. If the key is incorrect, the model’s
weights are not decrypted correctly and, therefore, the model does not achieve
sufficient accuracy. However, if the encryption key is hidden somewhere within
the program, an attacker may find this key through static analysis, decrypt the
model and thus gain access to the model.

6 D. Dorfmeister et al.
Attacks based on static analysis are possible as long as all data that is needed
to successfully run a program or model is contained within themselves. To counter
such attacks, essential data must be inaccessible. An example would be to prompt
a third party, e.g., the user or a PUF for the decryption key so it does not have
to be part of the program or model anymore.
3.2 Dynamic Analysis
Dynamic analysis is based on observing the behaviour and state of a program
or NN at runtime. This reaches from executing a program with various inputs
and observing its behaviour from the outside by, e.g., dumping its memory, to
employing a interactive disassembler. Interactive disassemblers enable the reverse
engineer to analyse a program at any time during its execution using breakpoints
and enables inspection of memory at any state.
Dynamic analysis enables an attacker to use data only present at runtime in
addition to information available from static analysis. Suppose a cryptographic
key is hidden successfully so that it cannot be retrieved by means of static analysis
and it is also hidden at runtime. The instructions of the program have to be
decrypted at some point while executing the program. However, an attacker can
wait until each instruction has been decrypted at least once and can thus recover
the full program. This also applies to NN. To successfully execute a NN, we must
know the internal structure of the NN as well as its assigned weights. Whenever
we need to perform some calculations using a weight, the correct, decrypted value
must be provided.
In this work, we focus on protection against static analysis. Therefore, our
goal is to remove critical information from the model and make it only available
at runtime. Providing a sound method that prevents static analysis is a first step
to secure NN models and already poses a significant challenge for attackers.
4 Copy Protection Method
The goal of our copy protection method is to prevent unauthorised copy and
use of pre-trained NN models. We propose the use of PUFs (see Section 2.2)
to encrypt some of the weights weassociated with the edges e∈E of an NN
model, so that the model only works correctly on its target machine. If used on
a different machine—even on a clone of the target machine—, the model will
drop its accuracy to levels that are determined by the number and selection of
encrypted weights. As we explained in Section 2.1, weights are learned from data
and are a key IP asset contained in any pre-trained NN model, making them an
ideal target for protection. The reader might ask why we encrypt just some of the
weights and not all of them. The answer is that this way our method can limit
the performance overhead caused by decryption and, as shown in this paper, still
provide an adequate level of protection.
More concretely, given a NN model Nwith set of edges Eand corresponding
weights wefor every e∈E , plus a PUF fwith domain Dffor a target machine

6 Evaluation
We choose four different NN models to evaluate our experiments. We train
these models ourselves following TensorFlow tutorials: Two of our models classify
images, one is based on the MNIST dataset5to detect handwritten digits, and the
other one on the Fashion MNIST dataset [ 18] to detect ten categories of clothing.
The other models recognise eight different predefined speech commands [ 17],
and positive or negative sentiment in IMDB reviews [ 9]. We encrypt a dense
layer of each image classification model. For the latter two models, we encrypt
one convolutional and one recurrent layer, respectively. For an overview of all
experiments, the models we use, and the total number of weights in the layers
we encrypt, see Table 1.
6.1 Accuracy
To show the degradation of accuracy in our models due to encryption, we randomly
select ten sets of weights containing 40 % of the weights per layer to be encrypted.
For each of these, we also collect data for subsets including fewer weights at
5 percentage point decrements. For comparison, we also measure the accuracy
at 0 % encryption, i.e., an unencrypted model. Figure 3 shows the mean of
the results of our experiments as well as their standard deviation. Note that
these results are only valid for executing the encrypted models without trying to
decrypt them.
For all experiments, the accuracy of the models drops significantly even at

Decryption on machines different from the target machine, e.g., cloned machines,
potentially further degrades the accuracy of the model. On these machines, the
PUF responses differ from those on the target machine and thus, decryption of
the encrypted weights fails. Effectively, the weights are encrypted once more,
potentially lowering the model’s accuracy even further.
6.2 Size Impact
The size of the actual NN model does not change during encryption. Nevertheless,
we need to store helper data containing the IDs of the encrypted weights and
their respective challenges for the PUF. With our PoC implementation, the size
of this data structure increases by 12 bytes per additional encrypted weight.
For example, the helper data for the model we use in experiment (a) at 20 %
encrypted weights, which yields a significant degradation of the model, requires
approximately 2.3 MiB of helper data, which could be further reduced by using a
more efficient way to identify the weights. The helper data must only be loaded
from disk during decryption, and it is not required to load this data into main
memory at once. Thus, even on embedded devices, the additional data should
not hinder the application of our approach.

7 Discussion
The used one-time key encryption mechanics in the form of Vernam that we
apply in this paper achievesperfectsecurity in a precise probability-theoretic
sense [ 2, Theorem 12.2]. This means that it is qualified to the best possible extent
regarding the secrecy property and the efficiency property of the encryption and
decryption algorithms. However, this only holds if the key is (a) truly randomly
selected, (b) used only once, and (c) as long as the plaintext. As usual in practice,
there are trade-offs in our adaptation to the case of protecting NN models.
In theory, we can meet properties (a) and (c) if the PUF fis injective with
domain and range {0,1}m, where mis the length of the binary representation of
the weights of the NN model N. In practice, we most probably need to replace the
“truly random” cipher key by a pseudorandom one, since PUFs are usually not
injective and shorter than the required length m. The same applies, for instance,
to the Vigen` ere encryption mechanism [ 2, Section 13.3], this inevitably results in
a less secure encryption. Property (b), on the other hand, can clearly be met, as
long as the key generation mechanism does not impose unacceptable overheads.
As our PoC implementation uses a simulated PUF and is not optimised for
performance, we did not conduct a performance evaluation. Nevertheless, it is
clear that the performance will be heavily influenced by the PUF response time
as well as the number of encrypted weights.
It is also apparent that there is a trade-off between performance overhead
and security level. This is determined by the desired drop in accuracy on the one
hand and the type of encryption on the other. If the model is only decrypted
once after loading (as per our PoC implementation), then the PUF response
time does not affect the runtime, only the loading time is affected. If we use
a more secure approach instead where each individual weight is decrypted on
demand for each processed input, and then encrypted again immediately after
use (possibly with a new key), then this will clearly have a negative impact in
the NN model’s performance. At the same time, the resulting protection would
have better resistance to sophisticated (dynamic) reverse engineering attacks.
In our PoC, we select weights at random and show that the encryption of
around 20 % of the weights is enough to obtain a sufficient degradation in the
accuracy of the NN models, and thus being able to apply the proposed copy
protection against static attacks. To offer protection against dynamic attacks
as outlined in the previous paragraph, but without affecting the performance
significantly, one could potentially encrypt/decrypt a substantially smaller number
of weight for each input processed by the NN model. This can still degrade the
accuracy of the NN model enough (see, e.g., [ 6,15]). We plan to investigate this
alternative in future research.
A final point that should be noted is that if attackers can somehow query the
PUF on the target machine to get the needed responses, then they can obviously
decrypt the network. There are, however, known ways to make PUFs resistant
to this type of attacks (see, e.g., [ 10,1]). Additionally, we could use obfuscation
techniques so that an attacker cannot easily identify where each PUF response is
used. There is also the possibility of considering Trusted Execution Environments

14 D. Dorfmeister et al.
(TEEs) for key operations or homomorphic encryption. Again, this needs to be
investigated in future work and will necessary involve a trade-off between security
and performance.
8 Related Work
Protecting the IP in NN models is of course not a completely new idea. Indeed,
several alternative methods already exist. In this section, we will discuss the most
relevant work in this sense.
We can identify two main approaches depending on how IP protection is
applied: (i) by means of different obfuscation techniques [ 7,20] that make it
sufficiently harder for an attacker to recover the original model, and (ii) by using
cryptography [ 12,8,3] to either encrypt the whole model, individual layers or,
as in our case, individual weights. In the remainder of this section, we discuss
each of these related techniques.
The Goldstein et al. [ 7] have shown that a good level of protection may
be achieved by applying various alterations to the structure of convolutional
filters in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs). To revert the applied
obfuscation, a secret key is needed. If an incorrect key is provided, the resulting
model will have a significantly lower accuracy than the original model.
Rakin et al. [ 13] explore the effects of applying bit flips induced by Rowhammer
attacks to a neural network. The authors use these bit flips to attack a model
and render it useless for other users. While this idea is not directly related to our
work, Zhao et al. [ 20] use a similar technique to protect neural networks. They
propose to calculate an error mask based on DRAM restore values that pose as a
unique physical property of individual DRAM modules. As such, the authors are
able to create an error mask that is bound to a specific DRAM module. They
proceed to use this error mask while training a neural network. The resulting
model is then bound to the DRAM module that will yield the correct error mask.
If executed on another DRAM module, the accuracy of the model is significantly
lower than the accuracy of the original model. The key difference to our approach
is that their model needs to be individually trained for each piece of hardware it
runs on while our work can be applied to any pre-trained model.
Cai et al. [ 3] apply encryption to only a small portion of the weights. They
apply the proposed encryption using a pre-calculated set of secret keys that are
stored in a separate key storage. The authors show that encrypting only a small
portion of the weights is enough to achieve a sufficient level of protection. In
contrast to our work, they rely on a set of keys that, if known to an attacker,
can be used to run the network at any arbitrary machine whereas our approach
is bound to specific hardware by using a PUF to generate secret keys while
encrypting and decrypting the model.
Making use of FPGAs to accelerate the execution time of neural networks is
a well known method. Guo et al. [ 8] propose to directly integrate their protection
into such an accelerator FPGA. They make use of a PUF that only yields the
correct results when executed on the correct FPGA. While their method seems

A PUF-Based Approach for Copy Protection of IP in NN Models 15
very promising, particularly regarding the low performance overhead associated
with the proposed protection, the solution is specifically tailored to convolutional
NNs running on FPGA hardware.
Finally, Pan et al. [ 12] use an Anderson PUF to incrementally encrypt layers
of a NN to efficiently bind it to specific hardware. They focus on analysing the
effectiveness of the protection to counteract fine-tuning attacks. This is a type
of attack that tries to approximate the original model from the obfuscated one
by making use of a fraction of the original training dataset. A key difference
to our approach is that they aim to render the behaviour of the protected
model equivalent to a random classifier. In contrast, our work has identified that
obfuscating only a small fraction of the weights is enough to achieve a good level
of protection against software piracy. Since we can limit the loss in accuracy to a
few percentage points, in theory we should be able to make our approach more
stealthy, which would in turn give us an advantage w.r.t. the fine-tuning attacks
considered in their work. The conjecture is that then it is not immediately obvious
for an attacker how the encrypted NN model produces the drop in performance.
This still needs to be confirmed by future research, though.
9 Conclusion
In this work, we presented a method to protect intellectual property in neural
network models from piracy. The main advantage of our approach is that NN
models cannot simply be copied to replicated machines, thus requiring reverse
engineering not just for the hardware but also the NN models. We evaluated
our method using different NN models and showed that they can be bound to
unique hardware properties in such a way that copying an NN model to another
machine renders it useless. Furthermore, this complicates a static analysis, since
without knowledge of the properties of the target hardware, i.e., PUF responses,
this mechanism cannot simply be removed.
A further step and planned future work is to make this protection more
robust against dynamic analysis. The current PoC implements the decryption
after loading, i.e., the entire model is decrypted and then stored decrypted in
main memory. A possible improvement in this respect would be to decrypt only
individual weights that are currently being used and then encrypt them again, or
to integrate this mechanism into a trusted execution environment. In addition, it
is also necessary to analyse and optimise performance and subsequently achieve
a good trade-off between performance and security, i.e., the number of weights
to be encrypted.

structure.title: A PUF-Based Approach for Copy Protection of Intellectual Property in Neural Network Models
structure.summary: This partial document introduces a novel approach for protecting intellectual property (IP) embedded in Neural Network (NN) models by binding them to specific hardware. The core problem addressed is the infeasibility of copying NN models to cloned hardware, which can be achieved by attackers replicating production machines. The proposed solution leverages Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs) to link an NN model's weights to unique and unclonable hardware properties. This binding ensures that the NN model can only achieve sufficient accuracy when executed on the original target hardware, thus preventing its proper functioning on any cloned hardware. The document states that the approach has been demonstrated to degrade accuracy on various NN models and outlines potential future improvements. The introduction further emphasizes the growing importance of NN models in industry and the significant investment in their development, making their IP a valuable target for protection.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.summary:
This partial document introduces a novel approach for protecting intellectual property (IP) embedded in Neural Network (NN) models by binding them to specific hardware. The core problem addressed is the ease with which NN models, representing valuable company IP, can be copied and used without authorization, leading to software piracy and financial losses.

The proposed solution leverages Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs), which are hardware-based security primitives that exploit unique, unclonable physical properties of circuits. The approach involves linking crucial NN model weights to the unique fingerprint generated by a PUF on the target hardware. This binding ensures that the NN model can only achieve sufficient accuracy when running on its designated hardware. If the NN model is copied to cloned hardware, the PUF response will differ, leading to a degradation in the model's accuracy, thus rendering unauthorized use ineffective.

The document outlines the motivation for this approach, differentiating it from traditional copy protection methods like passwords or hardware dongles, which are often easily circumvented. It emphasizes that the goal is to make copied models inaccurate rather than completely unusable, which can be a more subtle and effective protection mechanism with minimal runtime overhead for authorized use. The document also provides a conceptual illustration of how this protection works and its impact on model performance on both protected and cloned machines.

The paper is structured to first introduce the necessary background on NNs and PUFs, define the threat model, and then detail the proposed protection mechanism, its proof of concept, experimental results, and limitations.

nodes.title: Physically Unclonable Functions
nodes.summary:
The document discusses a PUF-based approach for copy protection of intellectual property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models. It explains that unauthorized copies of NN models can be detected and classified incorrectly by verifying a fingerprint via a Physically Unclonable Function (PUF). The paper is structured to first introduce background on NNs and PUFs, then specify the threat model, followed by the main contribution detailing the protection mechanism, proof of concept, experimental results, and discussion. The document also covers related work and conclusions.

Key concepts explained include:
*   **Neural Networks (NNs):** Their architecture, computation process, and the importance of protecting pre-trained models.
*   **Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs):** Functions based on unique physical hardware properties that are difficult to clone. They take a challenge (binary string) and produce a unique response (binary string) for a specific machine. Various types of PUFs are mentioned, including DRAM PUFs, arbiter PUFs, SRAM PUFs, ring oscillator PUFs, and optical PUFs.
*   **Threat Model:** The paper focuses on attacks aiming to remove copy protection through reverse engineering. It assumes an attacker can gain access to the model but not query the PUF directly for Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs). The encryption method is assumed to be public knowledge.
*   **Static Analysis:** A method where an attacker analyzes the software (including NN models) without executing it, potentially finding encryption keys hidden within the program.

structure.title: Threat Model
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a copy protection approach for Intellectual Property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models using Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs). It explains that a PUF acts as a hardware-specific function that takes a binary input (challenge) and produces a unique binary output (response) for a particular machine. The document mentions various types of PUFs, including DRAM PUFs, arbiter PUFs, SRAM PUFs, ring oscillator PUFs, and optical PUFs, and states that the choice of PUF depends on factors like availability, response time, and security strength.

The document then outlines the threat model, focusing on attacks aimed at removing copy protection through reverse engineering. It assumes attackers can access the model but not query the PUF to obtain Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs). The paper specifically considers a "static attacker" who has access to the model's binary or source code but cannot execute it. An example of static analysis is provided, where an attacker might find an encryption key hidden within the program to decrypt the model's weights. The document clarifies that attacks on hardware, side-channel attacks, and supply chain attacks are not considered in this paper, and that protection against dynamic analysis is a future research direction.

nodes.title: Static Analysis
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses a PUF-based approach for copy protection of Intellectual Property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models.

The main points covered are:

*   **Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs):** The document explains what PUFs are, describing them as hardware-based security primitives that generate unique responses to specific inputs (challenges) based on the physical characteristics of the hardware. It highlights that a PUF's response is only valid on its intended machine. Examples of PUFs like DRAM PUFs, arbiter PUFs, SRAM PUFs, ring oscillator PUFs, and optical PUFs are mentioned, with the choice depending on application-specific factors.
*   **Threat Model:** The paper focuses on attacks aimed at removing copy protection through reverse engineering. It assumes attackers can gain access to the model but not necessarily query the PUF directly to obtain Challenge-Response Pairs (CRPs). The document explicitly excludes hardware attacks like side-channel attacks and supply chain attacks, focusing on a "static attacker" who has access to the model's binary or source code.
*   **Static Analysis:** This section defines static analysis as examining software without executing it, allowing attackers to access all information present when the program is not running. An example is given where an attacker might find an encryption key hidden within the program to decrypt model weights. The document suggests that to counter static analysis, essential data should be inaccessible and potentially prompted from a third party like a PUF.
*   **Dynamic Analysis:** This section describes dynamic analysis as observing a program's behavior and state during runtime. It allows attackers to use data only present at runtime, in addition to static analysis information. The document notes that dynamic analysis can be used to recover encrypted program instructions or NN weights by observing them as they are decrypted during execution.
*   **Focus on Static Analysis:** The paper explicitly states its current focus is on protection against static analysis, aiming to remove critical information from the model and make it available only at runtime.
*   **Copy Protection Method:** The proposed method aims to prevent unauthorized copying and use of pre-trained NN models by using PUFs to encrypt some of the model's weights. This encryption ensures the model functions correctly only on its target machine. Using the model on a different machine, even a clone, will result in a significant drop in accuracy. The document justifies encrypting only a subset of weights to balance performance overhead and protection level.

nodes.title: Dynamic Analysis
nodes.summary: This partial document discusses methods for protecting Neural Network (NN) models from unauthorized access and copying. It contrasts two types of analysis: static analysis, which examines a program or model without executing it, and dynamic analysis, which observes behavior during runtime. The authors state their focus is on protection against static analysis, aiming to remove critical information from the model and make it accessible only at runtime. They then introduce their proposed copy protection method, which uses Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) to encrypt a subset of the NN's weights. This encryption ensures the model functions correctly only on its designated machine, significantly degrading accuracy on any other machine, even a clone. The document explains that encrypting only some weights balances protection with performance overhead.

structure.title: Copy Protection Method
structure.summary: This document excerpt discusses methods for protecting intellectual property (IP) in pre-trained Neural Network (NN) models, specifically focusing on preventing unauthorized copying and use. It contrasts static and dynamic analysis techniques used by attackers to extract information from models. The authors propose a copy protection method that utilizes Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) to encrypt a subset of the NN's weights. This encryption binds the model to a specific machine, causing its accuracy to drop significantly if used on unauthorized hardware. The method adapts Vernam encryption using PUF responses as keys, operating on the binary representation of weights. A Proof of Concept (PoC) implementation in Python and TensorFlow is described, demonstrating how to encrypt weights and evaluate the resulting model's accuracy degradation. The PoC highlights the trade-off between the percentage of encrypted weights, protection strength, and performance overhead.

structure.title: Proof of Concept
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a proof of concept (PoC) for a copy protection method for Neural Networks (NNs) using Python and TensorFlow. The core of the method involves encrypting a percentage of the weights in a selected layer of the NN.

The main points covered are:

*   **Encryption Process:** The document details the `encrypt_model` algorithm, which takes an NN model, a layer ID, a percentage of weights to encrypt (`pct`), and input data. It randomly selects a percentage of weights from the specified layer, generates a challenge using a PUF (Physically Unclonable Function), and XORs the challenge with the weight to create an encrypted weight. A `helper` vector stores the challenges for each encrypted weight. The accuracy of the model is evaluated before and after encryption to assess the impact of weight modification.
*   **Decryption Process:** The `decrypt_model` algorithm is presented, which requires the encrypted model, input data, and the `helper` vector. It loads the challenges and encrypted weights, uses the PUF to generate the original challenge response, and XORs it with the encrypted weight to recover the original weight. This process is designed to only work correctly on the target machine where the PUF responses match those used during encryption.
*   **PUF Implementation:** The PoC uses a simulated XOR arbiter PUF from the `pypuf` library for demonstration purposes. In a real-world scenario, an actual PUF on the target machine would be used.
*   **Evaluation Setup:** Four different NN models are used for evaluation: two for image classification (MNIST and Fashion MNIST), one for audio recognition, and one for text sentiment analysis. Specific layers (dense, convolutional, recurrent) are chosen for encryption.
*   **Accuracy Degradation:** The evaluation section discusses how encrypting a percentage of weights degrades the model's accuracy. Experiments show a significant drop in accuracy even with a small percentage of encrypted weights, making unauthorized copies of the model less effective. The accuracy is measured both before encryption and after decryption on the target machine, and compared to the accuracy on a cloned machine.

structure.title: Evaluation
structure.summary: This partial document describes an evaluation of neural network models with encrypted weights. It details four different neural network models used for image classification (digits and clothing), audio recognition (speech commands), and text recognition (sentiment analysis). The document explains that these models were trained using TensorFlow tutorials and specifies the type of layer encrypted in each model (dense, convolutional, or recurrent). It also presents a table summarizing the experimental setup, including the model type, layer, and number of weights. The evaluation focuses on the degradation of model accuracy due to encryption, with experiments measuring accuracy at different percentages of encrypted weights. The results indicate a significant drop in accuracy even with a small percentage of encrypted weights, leading to performance approximating a random classifier.

nodes.title: Accuracy
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes an evaluation of a PUF-based approach for copy protection of Intellectual Property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models. The main points covered are:

*   **Experimental Setup:** Four different NN models are used for evaluation: two for image classification (digits and clothing), one for audio recognition, and one for text recognition. Table 1 provides an overview of these models, their types, and the number of weights in the encrypted layers.
*   **Accuracy Degradation:** The document details experiments measuring the drop in model accuracy as a percentage of encrypted weights increases. It shows that accuracy significantly degrades even at low percentages of encryption, often approximating a random classifier. The text classification model, for instance, becomes ineffective with only 10-20% encrypted weights.
*   **Decryption and Machine Dependency:** The accuracy of the model is restored to its original level when decrypted on the target machine. However, if the encrypted model is used without decryption or decrypted on different (e.g., cloned) machines, the accuracy is lowered due to differing PUF responses.
*   **Size Impact:** While the NN model size itself doesn't change, storing helper data (IDs and challenges for PUF) for encrypted weights adds overhead. The document quantifies this overhead and suggests it's manageable, even for embedded devices.

nodes.title: Size Impact
nodes.summary: The provided document excerpt discusses the impact of encryption on the accuracy of image classifiers, particularly when decryption occurs on machines different from the target machine. It highlights that using cloned machines for decryption can further degrade accuracy due to differing PUF responses. The text also addresses the size impact of storing helper data for encrypted weights, noting that while it increases storage requirements, it can be managed even on embedded devices. The discussion section delves into the theoretical and practical aspects of PUF-based encryption for Neural Network (NN) models, including trade-offs between security, efficiency, and performance. It explains that while Vernam encryption offers perfect security theoretically, practical implementations using PUFs may require pseudorandom keys, leading to reduced security. The excerpt also touches upon the performance implications of decrypting weights on demand versus once after loading, and the potential for dynamic reverse engineering attacks. Finally, it mentions the possibility of attackers querying the PUF and suggests methods to mitigate this, such as PUF resistance techniques and obfuscation.

structure.title: Discussion
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt discusses a PUF-based approach for protecting Intellectual Property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models, focusing on copy protection. The main points covered are:

*   **Encryption Mechanics and Security:** The paper utilizes Vernam cipher for encryption, which offers perfect security under ideal conditions (truly random, single-use, and plaintext-length keys). However, practical adaptations for NN models involve trade-offs.
*   **PUF Limitations and Practicalities:** PUFs are generally not injective and may be shorter than the required key length, necessitating the use of pseudorandom keys, which reduces security. The single-use property of the key can be met if key generation overhead is acceptable.
*   **Performance vs. Security Trade-off:** There's a clear trade-off between performance overhead and security level. Decrypting weights on demand for each input significantly impacts performance but offers better resistance to dynamic attacks. Encrypting a smaller percentage of weights (around 20%) is sufficient for static attacks, while dynamic attack protection without significant performance impact might involve encrypting/decrypting fewer weights per input.
*   **PUF Vulnerabilities and Mitigation:** Attackers querying the PUF on the target machine can decrypt the network. Mitigation strategies include making PUFs resistant to such attacks, using obfuscation techniques, or employing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) or homomorphic encryption, all of which require further investigation and involve security-performance trade-offs.
*   **Related Work:** The document reviews existing IP protection methods for NN models, categorizing them into:
    *   **Obfuscation Techniques:** Altering model structure (e.g., convolutional filters) or using hardware-specific properties (e.g., DRAM error masks) to make reverse engineering difficult. These methods often require a secret key or are bound to specific hardware.
    *   **Cryptography:** Encrypting the whole model, individual layers, or individual weights. The paper contrasts its PUF-based key generation with methods that use pre-calculated secret keys stored separately, highlighting that its approach is hardware-bound. It also mentions integrating protection into hardware accelerators like FPGAs using PUFs.

structure.title: Related Work
structure.summary: This partial document discusses methods for protecting intellectual property (IP) in neural network (NN) models, focusing on preventing unauthorized copying and reverse engineering. It categorizes existing approaches into two main types: obfuscation techniques that make model recovery difficult and cryptographic methods that encrypt parts or all of the model. The document then reviews several related works, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses, particularly in comparison to the authors' own PUF-based approach. Key differences discussed include the hardware dependency of the protection, the scope of encryption (individual weights vs. layers), and the impact on model accuracy. The conclusion reiterates the advantage of their method in binding NN models to unique hardware properties, requiring reverse engineering of both hardware and software. Future work is planned to enhance robustness against dynamic analysis and optimize the performance-security trade-off.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a Physical Unclonable Function (PUF)-based approach for protecting intellectual property (IP) in Neural Network (NN) models from piracy. The core idea is to bind NN models to unique hardware properties, making them useless if copied to different machines without reverse-engineering both the hardware and the NN model. The method is designed to complicate static analysis, as the protection mechanism cannot be easily removed without knowledge of the target hardware's PUF responses.

The document also contrasts this approach with prior work by Pan et al. [12], which uses an Anderson PUF to incrementally encrypt NN layers and aims to make the protected model behave like a random classifier. The authors of this document argue that their method, by obfuscating only a small fraction of weights, can achieve good protection against software piracy with minimal loss in accuracy, potentially offering an advantage against fine-tuning attacks by making the performance drop less obvious to attackers.

Future work is planned to enhance robustness against dynamic analysis by decrypting individual weights as needed or integrating the mechanism into trusted execution environments. Optimizing performance and finding a good trade-off between performance and security (i.e., the number of encrypted weights) are also identified as necessary steps. The document concludes with a list of references.
